# Recipes

Each recipe below is a change to `config/TTpipeConfig.yaml` (or a command), with
what it does and what to watch out for. After any change, run
`bash TTpipe.sh -n` first: the dry run lists what Snakemake will redo.

## Analysis-only run on an existing count matrix

You already have a gene-by-sample count matrix (from TTpipe or elsewhere) and
want only DESeq2, GSEA, the Sankey and the report.

```yaml
run_processing: false
run_analysis: true
analysis_counts: '/path/to/counts.txt'
gtf: '/path/to/gencode.vM25.annotation.gtf'
```

- The matrix is tab-separated, the first column is `gene_id`, the header holds
  the sample `Name`s (the same format as `counts/counts_deseq2.txt`), and the
  values are integer counts.
- The samplesheet needs only `Name`, `Condition` and `Replicate` (no FASTQ
  columns). Every matrix column must equal a samplesheet `Name`, and vice versa;
  otherwise DESeq2 stops and lists the differences.
- `gtf` is still required: the gene table (`gene_info`) is built from it and the
  GSEA ranking needs gene symbols. The gene ids in the matrix must be the ones in
  the GTF (for example both with GENCODE version suffixes).
- With `run_processing: false` and an empty `analysis_counts`, TTpipe uses
  `<outputDir>/counts/counts_deseq2.txt` if it exists, and otherwise stops with a
  message.
- The QC report still runs (`qc_report: true`), limited to what a count matrix
  allows ([Reading the QC report](qc.qmd#when-a-section-is-skipped)).

The rule graph for this mode is in [Running](running.qmd#running-only-part-of-the-workflow).

## Processing only

Align, count and build tracks, and decide on the statistics later:

```yaml
run_analysis: false
```

You still get the counts, tracks and the QC report (with a PCA computed from
the counts). Setting `run_analysis: true` later runs only the analysis, because
the processing outputs already exist.

## Rerunning only the statistics after a change

To change `design`, `comparisons`, `alpha`, `min_count`, `gsea_*` or the
reference condition, edit the config and run the dry run. Snakemake sees the
changed parameters and redoes `deseq2` and what depends on it (`rnk`, `fgsea`,
`sankey`, the QC report); the alignment and counts are untouched.

## Per-sample tracks

By default only per-condition tracks (replicates merged) are made. For one
bigWig set per sample as well:

```yaml
sample_tracks: true
```

This adds `tracks/samples/<sample>.bw`, `<sample>_forward.bw` and
`<sample>_reverse.bw`. Their scale factor is the largest final read-pair count
among **all samples** divided by that sample's count; the `scale_factors` option
is not used for them. Use them to check replicate agreement in a browser.

## Trimming

The guide runs FastQC only and says to consider trimming if adapter content is
above 5 %. TTpipe therefore does not trim by default. To trim with fastp:

```yaml
trim: true
fastp_extra: ''          # extra fastp arguments, e.g. '--length_required 30'
```

fastp's defaults apply (automatic paired-end adapter detection, quality
filter, length filter) plus `fastp_extra`. STAR then aligns the trimmed reads;
FastQC still runs on the raw reads, and fastp's JSON goes into the MultiQC
page. The trimmed FASTQs are temporary. Changing `trim` after a run reruns the
alignment and everything after it.

## Strandedness: dUTP or forward

`strandedness` states how the library was made:

| Value | Meaning | Read 1 | Read 2 |
|-------|---------|--------|--------|
| `dUTP` (default) | dUTP second-strand protocols, including TTchem-seq; the guide's assumption | antisense to the transcript | sense |
| `forward` | read 1 is the sense read | sense | antisense |

It decides which read pairs go to `<sample>_forward.bam` (RNA transcribed from
the + strand) and which to `_reverse.bam`. Everything strand-specific follows:
the forward and reverse tracks, the per-strand counts and the "sense %" in the
QC report.

**How to check.** Run once and open the QC report's strandedness panel. With the
right setting most reads fall on the gene's own strand (the default warn level is
90 %). If the median across samples is low, and the report says most reads are on
the opposite strand, you chose the wrong one: switch the value.

**Switching.** Edit `strandedness`, run the dry run and then the pipeline.
Snakemake sees the changed parameters of `split_strands` and redoes it and
everything after it: the strand BAMs, the merged BAMs, tracks, HTSeq counts,
DESeq2 and the report. The alignment and deduplication are not redone.

A sample sheet whose libraries are a mix of both types is not supported:
`strandedness` is one setting for the whole run.

## Counting on the sense strand only

The HTSeq counts are made per strand (`counts_forward.txt`,
`counts_reverse.txt`); `count_strand` decides how they become the DESeq2
matrix `counts_deseq2.txt`:

```yaml
count_strand: 'sum'      # default
# count_strand: 'sense'
```

| Value | What it counts | Notes |
|-------|----------------|-------|
| `sum` | forward + reverse for each gene | Reads on either strand: includes antisense reads. This is what the guide's **code** does, and TTpipe's default |
| `sense` | forward counts for + genes, reverse counts for - genes | Drops reads on the opposite strand. This is what the guide's **text** describes. A gene with no +/- strand falls back to forward + reverse; a counted gene missing from `gene_info.tsv` is an error |

The two give different numbers. With `sum`, a gene's count includes
transcription of anything on the other strand that overlaps it (antisense
transcripts); with `sense` that is excluded, but a wrong `strandedness` would
now give wrong counts, while with `sum` it would not matter for the counts.
Choose deliberately and say which you used.

## Custom comparisons and design

By default every condition is compared with `reference_condition`. To choose
comparisons yourself, list `[treatment, reference]` pairs using the samplesheet
condition names:

```yaml
reference_condition: 'DMSO'
condition_order: ['DMSO', '2H', '6H', '24H']
comparisons: [['6H', '2H'], ['24H', '6H'], ['24H', 'DMSO']]
```

The result files are named `<treatment>_vs_<reference>` (here `6H_vs_2H`,
`24H_vs_6H`, `24H_vs_DMSO`). Rules for the list:

- every name must be a `Condition` in the samplesheet;
- `condition_order`, if given, must list **exactly** the samplesheet conditions;
- `reference_condition` must be one of them. It is the base level of the DESeq2
  factor and the reference of the default pairs; with explicit `comparisons`
  the results do not depend on it;
- when comparisons do not share one reference, the Sankey axes are labelled with
  the full comparison names.

To change the model, set `design`. The columns available are `condition` and
`replicate`, and the formula must include `condition`:

```yaml
design: '~ condition'                  # no batch term
# design: '~ condition + replicate'    # default (the guide's ~ time + replicate)
```

Use `~ condition` when replicates are independent and the same label (`rep1`)
in different conditions does not mean a shared batch. Anything else, such as a
column you added to the samplesheet, is rejected: only `condition` and
`replicate` are given to DESeq2.

## Pinning scale factors

Track heights are scaled so that conditions sequenced to different depths
compare fairly. By default the scale factor is computed: the largest
replicate-merged read-pair count among the conditions, divided by this
condition's. To use your own values for some conditions, for example to match a
published track set:

```yaml
scale_factors: {DMSO: 1.2757, 2H: 1}
```

Conditions you list use your number (shown as source `config` in
`tracks/scale_factors.tsv`); the rest are computed. The maximum is taken over
all conditions, including the ones you pinned. The values the guide quotes come
from the authors' repository
(<https://github.com/magnitov/zfp143>); get them from there rather than from
this book. A name that is not a condition is an error. Only the per-condition
tracks use this setting.

## Gene-set collections for GSEA

```yaml
gsea_collections:
  Hallmarks: '/path/to/mh.all.v2023.2.Mm.symbols.gmt'
  Reactome: '/path/to/m2.cp.reactome.v2023.2.Mm.symbols.gmt'
gsea_seed: 42
```

Each entry names a collection (used in the output file name, so use letters,
digits and `_`) and a `.gmt` file with gene symbols you downloaded yourself.
Empty `{}` skips GSEA. See [Differential expression and
GSEA](analysis.qmd#gsea-with-fgsea).

## Building or reusing the STAR index

```yaml
star_index: '/path/to/mm10_STARgenome'
build_star_index: true     # once
```

After it has been built, set `build_star_index: false` so the index is only
read. With `build_star_index: false`, `star_index` must already be an index. If
`build_star_index: true` and `star_index` is empty the index is built under
`<outputDir>/reference/star_index`. `sjdb_overhang` is the read length minus 1
and matters only when building.

## Use a spike-in (e.g. ERCC92) {#use-a-spike-in}

For libraries that contain a spike-in RNA. The module is **optional and
experimental**; the keys are in [Configuration](configuration.qmd#spike-in).

1. **Get the spike-in FASTA and GTF**, for example `ERCC92.fa` and `ERCC92.gtf`
   from the supplier (they are not in the repository). The FASTA may be plain or
   `.gz`. The GTF is optional, but without it there is no
   `counts/counts_spike.txt` and no `size_factor_method: 'genes'`. An exon-only
   GTF such as `ERCC92.gtf` is fine.
2. **Set the `spike_in` keys:**

   ```yaml
   spike_in:
     enabled: true
     fasta: '/path/to/ERCC92.fa'
     gtf: '/path/to/ERCC92.gtf'
     prefix: 'spike_'
     use_contigs: []
     normalize: ['tracks', 'deseq2']
     size_factor_method: 'total'
   ```

3. **Give STAR an index that contains the spike-in.** Either a new directory
   that TTpipe builds from the combined host plus spike-in reference:

   ```yaml
   star_index: '/path/to/GRCh38_ERCC_STARgenome'   # new, not your host-only index
   build_star_index: true
   ```

   or `build_star_index: false` with `star_index` pointing at an index already
   built from that combined reference (with the prefixed contig names). A
   host-only index is refused when the workflow is parsed. The build needs more
   memory than the host alone: 62.5 GB was measured for human plus ERCC92
   (mouse alone: about 29 GB).
4. **Choose `normalize` and `use_contigs`.** `['tracks']` sets only the bigWig
   factors; `['tracks', 'deseq2']` also the DESeq2 size factors (when
   `run_analysis` is true); `[]` only counts the spike-in. In `use_contigs`,
   list the spike-ins whose reads should set the factors, by their FASTA names
   (for example `['ERCC-00002', 'ERCC-00043']`). In TT-seq, where a mix of
   4sU-labeled and unlabeled spike-ins is common, list the labeled ones: only
   they go through the 4sU purification. Which ones are labeled comes from your
   protocol.
5. **Dry run:** `bash TTpipe.sh -n`. It should list `spike_reference`, one
   `spike_idxstats` per sample and `spike_summary`, and `spike_size_factors`
   when `deseq2` is in `normalize` and the analysis runs (and `star_index` when
   the index is built).
6. **Run**, then check the counts before using any factor:
   - `spike/spike_counts.tsv`: per sample `host_pairs`, `spike_pairs_all`,
     `spike_pairs_used` (only `use_contigs`) and `spike_pct`.
   - `spike/spike_contig_counts.tsv`: pairs per spike-in contig and sample.
     It shows which spike-ins actually received reads.
   - `tracks/scale_factors.tsv`: source `spike-in` with `tracks`, plus the
     `host_pairs` and `spike_pairs` columns.
   - With `deseq2`: `spike/size_factors.tsv` (method `total`) or
     `spike/control_genes.txt` (method `genes`), and
     `analysis/deseq2/deseq2_size_factors.tsv` with the factors DESeq2 used.
   - `counts/counts_spike.txt` holds the spike-in genes; the usual count
     matrices hold host genes only.

What has been run: this recipe with `normalize: ['tracks']` and
`use_contigs: []` on a human dataset with ERCC92 (2 million read pairs per
sample, processing only). Only six ERCC contigs received reads, 30 to 89 pairs
per sample, which is far too few for usable factors (Poisson noise alone is
about 10 to 18 %); it tested the mechanics. DESeq2 with spike-in factors and
`size_factor_method: 'genes'` have not been run on real data. The QC report
does not show spike-in numbers yet.

## A different organism or annotation

Everything genome-specific is in these keys:

```yaml
genome: 'hg38'                 # label only
genome_fasta: '/path/to/genome.fa'
gtf: '/path/to/annotation.gtf'
star_index: '/path/to/STARindex'
```

The FASTA and the GTF must come from the same source. `gene_info.py` reads
`gene_name` and `gene_type` (GENCODE) or `gene_biotype` (Ensembl) from the GTF;
rRNA % in the QC report needs genes typed `rRNA` or `Mt_rRNA`. TTpipe was set up
and its defaults chosen for mouse mm10 and GENCODE vM25; other genomes follow the
same code path. Human (GRCh38, GENCODE v44) has been run on real data for
processing only (no DESeq2 or GSEA); other genomes have not been tried.

## Turning optional outputs off

```yaml
multiqc: false      # skip the MultiQC page
qc_report: false    # skip the QC table and report
```

`multiqc_extra` passes extra arguments to MultiQC. The MultiQC page exists only
on processing runs.

## Plot my genes of interest, lncRNAs or enhancers {#plot-my-genes}

The stranded signal page (`analysis/TTpipe_stranded_signal.html`,
[how to read it](analysis.qmd#stranded-signal)) draws the stranded bigWigs for
the loci you choose. It is built by default; you only say where to look.

Genes by name or by position:

```yaml
track_loci: ['Gapdh', 'Myc', 'ENSMUSG00000057666', 'chr1:3000000-3010000']
```

A list of lncRNAs or any gene set: put one symbol per entry in `track_loci`, or
write a BED file with one region per line (`chrom`, `start`, `end`, optional
`name`, `score`, `strand`; start is 0-based as in any BED file) and point to it:

```yaml
track_regions_bed: '/path/to/my_regions.bed'
```

Candidate enhancers, and their metagene profile (the strand column, if present,
orients the regions; without it the page shows + strand and - strand RNA, not
sense and antisense):

```yaml
track_regions_bed: '/path/to/enhancers.bed'
metagene_bed: '/path/to/enhancers.bed'
```

Then run the workflow again; only the `stranded_signal` rule is redone. The
page lists anything it could not find. `track_max_loci` (default 40) caps the
number of tracks; the metagene uses every region of `metagene_bed`.

Be clear about what this does. **TTpipe does not call enhancer RNAs**: it only
shows the stranded signal where you point it, and the metagene of a BED is the
average over your regions. Nascent enhancer transcripts are short and weak, so
a visible signal needs enough sequencing depth, a region list you trust, and
normally a comparison with a control region set; a BED of regions with no
signal gives a flat line, not a negative result about enhancers in general.
The signal is normalized by library size, unless the optional, experimental
spike-in module sets the track factors ([Use a spike-in](#use-a-spike-in)).

The page has been run on real data (mouse, and human processing only) as well
as synthetic data, but not on full-depth samples.

## Changing tool settings

| Key | Passes to | Example |
|-----|-----------|---------|
| `star_extra` | STAR alignment (guide: defaults) | `'--outFilterMismatchNmax 6'` |
| `min_mapq` | `samtools view -q` (guide: 10) | `10` |
| `remove_duplicates` | Picard `REMOVE_DUPLICATES` (guide: `true`) | `false` to only mark |
| `picard_extra` | Picard | `'VALIDATION_STRINGENCY=LENIENT'` |
| `bigwig_bin_size` | `bamCoverage --binSize` | `50` |
| `bigwig_extra` | `bamCoverage` | `'--extendReads'` |
| `htseq_nonunique` | `htseq-count --nonunique` | `all` |

The values in the Example column are illustrations of the syntax; the defaults
are the guide's. A Java heap option for Picard has not been verified to work
through `picard_extra`; the rule sets no heap, so Picard uses the JVM default.

## Reporting only

To rebuild the QC report from what exists on disk without building anything
else:

```yaml
run_processing: false
run_analysis: false
qc_report: true
```

Every metric whose files are missing is left blank and listed under "Skipped".
